title: SLO pacing savings snapshot
content:
Purpose and quick summary:

This note is a concise snapshot of a small bench run exploring the tradeoffs of proactive request pacing (a lightweight micro-scheduler that delays small requests by short windows) versus immediate dispatch. Goal: estimate measurable cost savings and p95/p99 SLA impacts for mixed interactive workloads (chat + embeddings) and produce a simple collateral page we can iterate into console docs.

Key summary bullets (TL;DR):
- Pacing window of 8–25ms applied to small completions reduces per-token cost by 9–18% in our test harness while increasing p95 by 5–12% and p99 by 8–20% depending on model size and session mix.
- Greatest wins when traffic has high spike fraction but low median length (support chat, short queries). Minimal benefit for sustained long-generation workloads.
- Savings amplify when combined with small KV cache hit rates (>15%) and 4x batching opportunity.

Experiment setup (quick):
- Date: runs 2027-09-20 to 2027-09-22.
- Cluster: ded-nyc1 (A100s), single pool, isolated quota to avoid noisy neighbors.
- Models: rdlw-7B-int8 (7B quantized), rdlw-13B-q4 (13B q4), rdlw-70B-q4 (70B q4/kernels).
- Workloads: two synthetic mixes recorded from production samples:
  * mix-A (short-chat): 70% requests <= 60 tokens, 25% requests 60-300, 5% > 300.
  * mix-B (assistant-heavy): 40% <=60, 30% 60-400, 30% >400.
- Baseline: immediate dispatch (no pacing) + auto-batching (window 0ms, batch up to 32).
- Pacing modes tested: 8ms, 15ms, 25ms hold-before-dispatch; opportunistic coalescing into batch if another request arrives within window.
- Measurement: per-request latencies recorded at client-observed (end-to-end) and per-token GPU time from runtime traces. Cost is estimated from amortized GPU time + fixed infra overhead converted to $/1k tokens by internal unit pricing.

Representative results (aggregated median across 6 runs each):

Text table: p95/p99 and cost per 1k tokens
Model | Mix | Mode | p50 (ms) | p95 (ms) | p99 (ms) | $/1k tokens | savings vs baseline
rdlw-7B-int8 | mix-A | baseline | 85 | 220 | 320 | 0.0098 | 0%
rdlw-7B-int8 | mix-A | pace-8ms | 93 | 230 | 340 | 0.0089 | 9.2%
rdlw-7B-int8 | mix-A | pace-15ms | 100 | 245 | 370 | 0.0086 | 12.2%
rdlw-7B-int8 | mix-A | pace-25ms | 110 | 260 | 410 | 0.0080 | 18.4%

rdlw-13B-q4 | mix-A | baseline | 140 | 360 | 520 | 0.0174 | 0%
rdlw-13B-q4 | mix-A | pace-8ms | 150 | 375 | 540 | 0.0159 | 8.6%
rdlw-13B-q4 | mix-A | pace-15ms | 162 | 395 | 590 | 0.0152 | 12.6%
rdlw-13B-q4 | mix-A | pace-25ms | 180 | 430 | 680 | 0.0144 | 17.2%

rdlw-70B-q4 | mix-A | baseline | 420 | 980 | 1600 | 0.068 | 0%
rdlw-70B-q4 | mix-A | pace-8ms | 435 | 1010 | 1680 | 0.062 | 8.8%
rdlw-70B-q4 | mix-A | pace-15ms | 455 | 1050 | 1770 | 0.058 | 14.7%
rdlw-70B-q4 | mix-A | pace-25ms | 492 | 1120 | 1940 | 0.054 | 20.6%

(Notes: $/1k tokens includes an internal infra overhead multiplier; absolute prices are illustrative relative numbers for comparing modes.)

Observations and interpretation:
- Small models (7B) show highest relative improvement in unit-cost with modest latency impact — these are the easiest wins for early rollout of pacing as an opt-in knob for low-latency tiers.
- Larger models have larger absolute latency increases at p99 for higher windows, but also larger dollar savings per token (because their baseline $/1k is higher). Decide by SLA tier whether percent savings justify tail increases.
- Mix sensitivity: mix-B (assistant-heavy) reduced savings by ~40% across models because longer generations reduce opportunities to coalesce short requests. We should highlight that pacing is workload-dependent.

Simple ASCII chart: relative savings vs p95 increase (mix-A)

Model   | 8ms  | 15ms | 25ms
rdlw-7B | +9% (p95 +4.5%) | +12% (p95 +11%) | +18% (p95 +18%)
rdlw-13B| +8.6% (p95 +4%)  | +12.6% (p95 +9.7%)| +17.2% (p95 +19%)
rdlw-70B| +8.8% (p95 +3%)  | +14.7% (p95 +7%)  | +20.6% (p95 +14%)

Collateral language draft for console docs (short):
"Proactive pacing is a lightweight scheduling knob that introduces a short, configurable delay (8–25ms) for very small requests to increase natural batching and reduce per-token GPU costs. For conversational workloads dominated by short queries, our tests show pacing can reduce unit cost by up to ~20% with small increases to tail latency. Pacing is workload-dependent — enable for low-median-length traffic or in combination with prefix caching for best results."

Tradeoffs and recommended defaults (proposal):
- "latency-sensitive" SLA: disable pacing by default (customers with strict p99 targets).
- "cost-balanced" SLA: enable 8ms pacing default with opt-out; monitor p95 and p99 for regressions.
- "throughput-optimized" SLA (background jobs, batchy workloads): enable 25ms + larger batching cap.

Runtime notes / instrumentation we used:
- client-observed latencies were recorded in dev-clients instrumented with trace ids.
- runtime trace tags used: batch_size, batch_wait_ms, kv_cache_hit, kernel_type.
- we used a lightweight sampling of traces (1/50) to compute p99 to reduce tracing overhead.

Quick checklist for a formal benchmark page (next steps):
- Run full sweep across regions (nyc, syd, fra) and repeat at 3 different sustained load levels (20%, 60%, 110% of pool capacity).
- Add production trace sampling (anonymized) to estimate real-world mix-A prevalence.
- Add cost model sensitivity to cloud provider pricing changes (gpu hour assumptions) and our reserved pool amortization.
- Draft console toggles UI copy and include a short experiment generator in the console (simulate expected savings given your traffic shape).

Open questions / discussion items:
- Is a fixed hold window better than a percentile-based hold (hold until x ms or until n requests queued)?
- Should pacing be adaptive to recent observed batch arrival rates per shard? (adaptive ~ predictive scheduler)
- Risk: on-cold path where a single client sends time-critical small messages (low tolerance for extra ms). Need per-route opt-out.

Raw artifacts and links (where to find traces / scripts):
- bench scripts: github:repo/runtime/bench/pacing-sim
- runtime traces (anonymized): s3://redwood-bench/pacing/2027-09-20/ (owner has access)
- short dashboard prototype (internal): confluence:INFR-ops-slo-pacing-v2#dashboard

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working snapshot intended for product + runtime teams to decide if we should A/B in a small customer cohort. Please add comments inline or ping me on #eng-console. I can run the regional sweeps once we agree on a measurement checklist.

-- Aisha

"Notes to self": consider adding a micro-case where we pair pacing with response-chunking (emit first chunk immediately then pace later bits) — might recover p50 while keeping batching benefits.
